column3: Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew calls those arriving “the people”; BSB specifies “the troops” and makes their arrival a return. It says the ark will come “into our midst,” rendered “go with us” in BSB.
The Hebrew leaves the people sent unnamed and has no separate “back”; BSB supplies “men” and “back.” It also supplies “between” in describing the LORD’s place among the cherubim.
The Hebrew repeats the shouting root in the verb and “a great shout”; BSB expresses it as raising a shout.
The Hebrew repeats “the sound of the shout”; BSB varies the second occurrence as “loud shouting.”
The Hebrew’s coming verb is singular with Elohim; BSB uses plural “The gods have entered.” The time expression literally says “yesterday, the day before yesterday,” rendered “before” in BSB.
The Hebrew names Egypt collectively; BSB uses “the Egyptians.” It has singular “every plague,” rendered “all kinds of plagues” in BSB.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew uses plural “his tents” distributively for each fleeing man; BSB uses singular “his tent.”
Close to the Hebrew.

Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew asks what the sound of this tumult is; BSB renders this as “Why this commotion?”
The Hebrew joins the fixed eyes and inability to see with “and”; BSB makes the latter an explicit “because” clause.
The Hebrew repeats “the battle line” as the place fled from; BSB substitutes “there.” It leaves the questioner unnamed, where BSB supplies Eli.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew leaves Eli unnamed twice and describes his neck as being broken; BSB names Eli twice and says “he broke his neck.”
The Hebrew refers to “his daughter-in-law” without naming Eli; BSB supplies his name.
The Hebrew says she did not “set her heart” on the words; BSB renders this bodily expression as not paying heed.
The Hebrew refers simply to her father-in-law and husband after naming the ark’s capture; BSB supplies the explicit statement that they “had been killed.”
Close to the Hebrew.
